claims.text: Conventionally processed eutectic or in situ composite high-entropy alloys typically contain straight lamellar structures.
Controlled post-solidification deformation or thermomechanical processing can transform straight lamellae into a vermicular, kinked morphology.
Kinking straight lamellae into a vermicular morphology introduces additional phase boundaries in varied orientations.
The additional interphase boundaries created by vermicular lamellae pin dislocations.
The additional interphase boundaries created by vermicular lamellae arrest crack propagation.
Increasing the density and spatial heterogeneity of phase boundaries impedes or decouples dislocation motion.
A heterogeneous lamellar structure delays microcrack initiation or promotes microcrack arrest.
Vermicular boundaries enable the soft FCC phase to carry more deformation and exploit the strain-hardening capacity of all phases.
The vermicular morphology will improve both strength and ductility relative to straight-lamellar eutectic high-entropy alloys.
The proposed treatment will increase yield strength and ultimate tensile strength by approximately 20–30%.
The proposed treatment will increase uniform elongation.
The proposed treatment will increase or maintain Young's modulus.
The proposed treatment will significantly improve fracture resistance.
Straight-lamellar baseline alloys have a lower density of heterogeneously oriented phase boundaries than the proposed vermicular material.
The strategy is applicable primarily to multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloys that already possess lamellar structures.
The strategy is unlikely to benefit single-phase or amorphous high-entropy alloys.
Temperature, strain rate, and annealing conditions can be optimized to induce lamellar kinking without forming coarse phases or causing embrittlement.
The long-term stability of the vermicular morphology under cyclic loading or extreme environments has not been established.
Identically composed treated and straight-lamellar control samples can be compared using tensile, modulus, and fracture-toughness tests.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in strength, ductility, Young's modulus, and fracture resistance would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis asserts improved Young's modulus, whereas the predicted outcome allows Young's modulus merely to be maintained.

The 20–30% numerical prediction is stated only for yield and ultimate tensile strength, but the falsification rule ambiguously applies roughly 20–30% improvement to strength, ductility, Young's modulus, and fracture resistance. It also requires an improvement in Young's modulus even though the predicted outcome permits no change.
